title: Stabilization of Ferroelectric Domains via Interfacial Strain in HoFeO3- BaTiO3 Nanofiber Heterostructures for Enhanced Hybrid Energy Harvesting
authors: Smita Chaturvedi, Swathi Krishna, Shivshankar Jokare, Supriya Sahoo, Vikash Kushwaha, Priyank Shyam, Mandar Shirolkar, R. Boomishankar
abstract: Piezoelectric nanogenerators (PENGs) are an attractive platform for self-powered mechanical-energy harvesting, but their output is often limited by depolarization fields, charge leakage, and inefficient stress transfer to the active dipoles, particularly in polymer-dominated composites. Here we report HoFeO3-BaTiO3 (HFO-BTO) nanofiber heterostructures prepared by alternating sol-gel electrospinning, in which orthorhombic HoFeO3 (Pbnm) and tetragonal BaTiO3 (P4mm) coexist in intimate contact. Rietveld-refined X-ray diffraction, high-resolution transmission electron microscopy, and Raman spectroscopy indicate interfacial lattice distortion. Polarization-electric field loops show that the heterostructure retains a polarization comparable to that of BaTiO3 (16.39 vs 15.80 microcoulombs per square centimeter at zero field) while its switching-current maximum moves to a higher field (about 7 vs about 3.5 kilovolts per centimeter), consistent with strain-stabilized ferroelectric domains. When the nanofibers are encapsulated in polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) and excited under cyclic impact, the device produces a hybrid output: the piezoelectric response of the strained BaTiO3 is supplemented by a triboelectric contribution from contact electrification. The HFO-BTO device delivers open-circuit voltage peaks of about +6 volts and -8 volts and a power density of 24.31 microwatts per cubic centimeter at a 4.7 megaohm load. This is 2.4 times the value for an identically fabricated BaTiO3 device (10.00 microwatts per cubic centimeter) and 8.7 times that of the HoFeO3 device (2.78 microwatts per cubic centimeter). These results link interface-driven lattice distortion to improved electromechanical output and identify all-oxide nanofiber heterostructures as a promising route to lead-free energy harvesting.
summary: This research reports on enhancing energy harvesting by creating HoFeO3-BaTiO3 nanofiber heterostructures. By engineering the interface between the two ferroelectric oxides, the researchers induced lattice strain that stabilized the ferroelectric domains. This resulted in a hybrid nanogenerator that achieved significantly higher power density by combining piezoelectric and triboelectric energy conversion.
main_problem: To develop efficient, self-powered mechanical-energy harvesting devices by improving the performance of piezoelectric nanogenerators (PENGs).
main_result: The HFO-BTO heterostructure significantly enhanced the power density (24.31 µW cm-3) compared to single-phase materials, demonstrating that interface-driven lattice distortion is key to improved electromechanical output.
method: The study involved synthesizing HFO-BTO nanofibers via alternating sol-gel electrospinning, characterizing them structurally (XRD, TEM), and testing them as hybrid nanogenerators under cyclic mechanical impact.
model_or_system: The physical system is the HoFeO3-BaTiO3 (HFO-BTO) nanofiber heterostructure, which is fabricated into a nanogenerator and encapsulated in PDMS. The performance relies on the coupling between the piezoelectric effect (from strained BaTiO3) and the triboelectric effect.
key_observables: Open-circuit voltage peaks (+6 V and -8 V), power density (24.31 µW cm-3), polarization-electric field loops, and interfacial lattice distortion.
important_parameters: The ratio of HFO to BTO phases, the applied mechanical strain/impact frequency, and the resulting coercive field strength.
main_assumptions: The total energy output is modeled as a hybrid sum of the piezoelectric contribution (from strained BaTiO3) and the triboelectric contribution (from contact electrification).
figures_summary: Figures likely show XRD patterns confirming phase formation, TEM images showing dual-phase integration, and electrical characterization plots (e.g., Power density vs. load resistance) comparing HFO, BTO, and HFO-BTO devices.
paper_structure: The paper follows a structure of problem identification (PENG limitations), material engineering (HFO-BTO synthesis and characterization), mechanism elucidation (interface strain stabilizing ferroelectric domains), and final device testing/performance benchmarking.
why_interesting: While primarily materials science, the study of strain-induced phase stabilization and the coupling of multiple physical effects (piezoelectric, ferroelectric, triboelectric) at interfaces is relevant to understanding complex, non-linear energy conversion systems, which can sometimes be modeled using advanced open quantum system approaches.

figures.caption: Figure 1. (a) Rietveld-refined XRD patterns of BTO, the HFO-BTO heterostructure, and HFO nanofibers (offset for clarity). Vertical tick marks indicate allowed reflections for tetragonal BaTiO3 (P4mm) and orthorhombic HoFeO3 (Pbnm); asterisks (*) denote trace Ho2O3 and α-Fe2O3 secondary- phase reflections. (b) Polyhedral crystal structure of tetragonal BaTiO3 (P4mm), showing the off- center displacement of Ti4+ within the TiO6 octahedron. (c) Crystal structure of orthorhombic HoFeO3 (Pbnm), with corner-sharing FeO6 octahedra and Ho3+ in the distorted A-site cavity (effectively eight- coordinate).

Figure 2. Calculated valence charge-density maps for (left to right) bulk HFO, the HFO|HFO-BTO interface, the BTO|HFO-BTO interface, and bulk BTO, viewed along the (100) and (010) projections. The pronounced accumulation of charge density in the Ti-O bond region at the heterointerface (compared with bulk BTO) indicates strengthened Ti 3d-O 2p hybridization at the interface.

Figure 3. TEM, HRTEM, SAED, and EDS elemental mapping of (a) HoFeO3, (b) BaTiO3, and (c) HFO-BTO heterostructure nanofibers. HRTEM panels (a2, b2, c2) show lattice fringes indexed to the respective phases; (a3, b3, c3, c4) are SAED patterns confirming crystallinity and coherent dual-phase integration; (a4, b4, c5) are EDS elemental maps (Ho, Fe, O for HFO; Ba, Ti, O for BTO; all five elements for HFO-BTO) demonstrating uniform composition and successful heterostructure formation.

Figure 4. (Top) Deconvoluted Raman spectra of HFO, HFO-BTO heterostructure, and BTO nanofibers, with phase-wise mode assignment indicated. (Bottom) Schematic eigen-displacement patterns of the principal FeO6 (left) and TiO6 (right) vibrational modes, illustrating the atomic motions responsible for the observed peaks. Systematic shifts in the heterostructure spectra relative to single- phase references evidence interfacial strain-induced lattice distortion.

Figure 5. Magnetization-field (M-H) loops of BTO, HFO, and HFO-BTO nanofibers at (a) 300 K and (c) 5 K, with magnified low-field views (b) and (d) highlighting the weak ferromagnetic hysteresis. The heterostructure retains a robust orthoferrite-derived hysteresis loop, confirming structural integrity of the FeO6 framework after co-annealing.
